_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 600 words, six questions in text order). Test 7 mixes the question types: attitude, inference, one reference question ('it'), one purpose question ('Why does the writer mention…?'), the meaning of a phrase and a final question that links the ending back to the opening (the new boots). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page and by Full test 7.
title: Above the tree line
subtitle: Ruth Calder spent twelve years in an insurance office before she became a mountain guide. Journalist Tom Ashby spent a day on the hills with her.

cards.text: I had been warned that Ruth Calder does not like to waste daylight, so I arrived at the car park at six. She was already there, sitting on the bonnet of a muddy van and eating a banana with the calm of someone who has never once been late. I had packed my rucksack three times the night before and still forgotten my gloves. She looked at my brand-new boots, then at my face, and said nothing at all. I found this far more alarming than any comment she could have made, and I spent the first hour of the walk trying to look experienced.
cards.question: How did the writer feel when he first met Ruth?
choices: Guilty that he had kept her waiting in the car park.
Relieved that she did not criticise his new boots.
Anxious about what she might be thinking of him.
Annoyed that she had not offered to lend him gloves.
cards.highlight: I found this far more alarming than any comment she could have made
cards.why: Her silence was 'far more alarming than any comment', so he spent an hour 'trying to look experienced'. B turns that alarm into relief; he arrived at six as warned, so nothing suggests he was late.

cards.text: Until she was thirty-four, Ruth worked as a claims assessor for an insurance company in Leeds. Her job was to decide, from photographs and forms, whether accidents had really happened in the way people said they had. She was good at it, she tells me, and well paid for it, and for years that seemed enough. 'I spent all day reading about other people's disasters,' she says, 'without ever going anywhere near one.' The change, when it came, was not dramatic. A friend persuaded her to join a weekend climbing course in Wales. By Sunday evening she had looked up what it would take to qualify as a guide.
cards.question: What does the writer suggest about Ruth's previous job?
choices: She found it dull from the very beginning.
It kept her at a distance from real experience.
She left it because she was not very good at it.
It involved visiting the places where accidents happened.
cards.highlight: without ever going anywhere near one
cards.why: She judged accidents 'from photographs and forms', 'without ever going anywhere near one', so D is the opposite. 'She was good at it' rules out C, and 'for years that seemed enough' rules out A.

cards.text: Qualifying took her four years. Mountain guiding, it turns out, involves much more than knowing the way up. There were logbooks to fill with hundreds of climbs, first-aid exams and winter assessments in conditions she describes as 'like being inside a washing machine full of gravel'. She failed one assessment and had to wait a whole year to take it again. Plenty of people, she admits, give up at that stage. What kept her going was surprisingly practical. 'I'd sold my flat to pay for it,' she says. 'Going back to insurance would have meant explaining that to my mother.'
cards.question: What does 'it' refer to in 'I'd sold my flat to pay for it'?
choices: the winter assessment she had to take again
the weekend course in Wales
the year she had to wait
the training needed to become a guide
cards.why: The whole paragraph describes the four years of 'qualifying', and that is what the flat paid for. The failed assessment is only one part of it, which makes A tempting but too narrow.

cards.text: By ten o'clock we were on the ridge, and I had stopped trying to look experienced. Ruth moves in a way I can only describe as unhurried; she never seems to be going fast, yet I was always slightly behind. Every few minutes she stopped, apparently to admire the view, and asked me a question: what I had eaten for breakfast, whether my sister had children. It was only later that I realised she had been listening to my breathing, not my answers. 'If someone can't finish a sentence,' she told me afterwards, 'we slow down. They never notice.'
cards.question: Why does the writer mention Ruth's questions about his breakfast and his sister?
choices: to show that she was quietly checking how he was coping
to suggest that she preferred chatting to climbing
to explain why they fell behind on the ridge
to show that she was mainly interested in the view
cards.highlight: she had been listening to my breathing, not my answers
cards.why: The questions were a test: 'she had been listening to my breathing, not my answers'. She only stopped 'apparently to admire the view', so D takes the cover story for the real reason.

cards.text: The hardest section was a narrow, broken edge that Ruth calls the Staircase. Here she roped us together, and for twenty minutes my world shrank to the next handhold. At one point I froze, convinced that the rock under my foot was about to give way. Ruth did not tell me it was safe. Instead, she asked me to describe exactly what I could feel. By the time I had found the words, my foot had stopped shaking. 'People think my job is getting clients to the top,' she said later. 'Mostly it's getting them out of their own heads.'
cards.question: What does Ruth mean by 'getting them out of their own heads'?
choices: making clients stop thinking about the view
helping clients escape from their own frightened thoughts
helping clients forget their problems at work
persuading clients to trust her judgement instead of their own
cards.highlight: By the time I had found the words, my foot had stopped shaking.
cards.why: Describing what he could feel pulled him away from the fear, and 'my foot had stopped shaking'. D is wrong because 'Ruth did not tell me it was safe': she never asked him to rely on her opinion.

cards.text: We reached the summit just after one, ate cheese sandwiches in a bitter wind, and were back at the van by five. As she unlaced her boots, I asked whether she ever missed the office, the salary, the heating. She thought about it for longer than I expected. 'I still assess risk all day,' she said eventually. 'The difference is that now I'm there when it happens.' Then she glanced at my boots, which were no longer new, and said they'd do. It was, I realised on the drive home, the first thing she had said about them all day, and I was absurdly pleased.
cards.question: What does the final paragraph suggest about the writer?
choices: He was disappointed that Ruth had not praised him more.
He believed Ruth secretly regretted leaving her office job.
He felt that he had finally won Ruth's approval.
He had decided to buy better boots for his next climb.
cards.why: The boots take us back to her silent look in the car park; 'they'd do' is small praise, but he was 'absurdly pleased'. She says she 'still assess[es] risk' and is now 'there when it happens', which shows no regret.
